title: Why You'd Never Want to Fall Into Jupiter
screen_title: Why You'd Never Want to Fall Into Jupiter
subtitle: A planet with no ground at all
yt_title: Why You'd Never Want to Fall Into Jupiter
intro: Jupiter is the giant of our solar system, with no surface to stand on. What would happen if you fell in? We dive through its radiation belts, its colorful clouds, the Great Red Spot, the ammonia hail and the crushing ocean of metallic hydrogen, follow the one probe that tried, and visit the moons that might hide life.

segments.text: Jupiter is the biggest planet in our solar system. And it has no ground. If you fell in, you would never land. So what would happen to you on the way down?
Welcome to Next Stop: Universe. If you enjoy calm, easy-to-follow journeys through space, tap subscribe. Today we fall into Jupiter. Hold on tight.

visual.query: A Dark Sky Full of Light (horalek-vst-milky-way)

segments.text: Jupiter is about eleven times wider than Earth. More than thirteen hundred Earths could fit inside it.
It's mostly hydrogen and helium, like a star. If it had been around eighty times heavier, it might have become one.
segments.headline: Almost a star

segments.text: And it spins fast. A day on Jupiter lasts less than ten hours. The fastest spin of any planet.
That spin stretches its clouds into colorful bands, the light zones and dark belts you can see in any picture.

files: Hubble Takes Close-up Portrait of Jupiter.png
visual.query: Hubble Takes Close-up Portrait of Jupiter

segments.headline: Belts and zones

segments.text: In sixteen ten, Galileo Galilei pointed one of the first telescopes at Jupiter and saw four tiny moons circling it. It proved that not everything in the sky goes around the Earth.

files: Jupiter Family of Moons by Juno.png
visual.query: Jupiter Family of Moons by Juno

segments.headline: Galileo, 1610

segments.text: Jupiter even has faint rings, made of fine dust, discovered by Voyager one in nineteen seventy-nine.
segments.headline: Hidden rings

segments.text: And its gravity is so strong that it pulls in comets. In nineteen ninety-four, comet Shoemaker-Levy nine broke into pieces and crashed into Jupiter, one after another, for almost a week.
segments.headline: A comet crashes, 1994

segments.text: Some of the dark scars left by the impacts were bigger than the whole Earth.
But before you even reach the clouds, there's a problem. Jupiter's magnetic field is about twenty thousand times stronger than Earth's.

files: Hubble Takes Close-up Portrait of Jupiter.png
visual.query: Hubble Takes Close-up Portrait of Jupiter

segments.headline: A giant magnet

segments.text: It traps charged particles in enormous radiation belts, the most intense in the solar system.

files: Jupiter and Io - NASA's Cassini in 2001 (51758670356).png
visual.query: Jupiter and Io - NASA's Cassini in 2001 (51758670356)

segments.headline: Deadly radiation

segments.text: Near the moon Europa, an unprotected person would get a deadly dose of radiation in about a day.

visual.label: to a deadly dose near Europa

segments.text: NASA's Juno spacecraft, which arrived in twenty sixteen, protects its electronics inside a vault of titanium. You would need one too.

files: Jupiter and the Great Red Spot - Juno Perijove 7.png
visual.query: Jupiter and the Great Red Spot - Juno Perijove 7

segments.headline: A titanium vault

segments.text: Now let's fall. Jupiter's gravity pulls you in faster and faster.

files: Jupiter and the Great Red Spot - Juno Perijove 7.png
visual.query: Jupiter and the Great Red Spot - Juno Perijove 7

segments.headline: Falling

segments.text: By the time you hit the top of the atmosphere, you'd be moving at about sixty kilometers per second. Faster than any spacecraft has ever entered Earth's air.
The friction would turn you into a blazing fireball in seconds. Only a heat shield could survive it.
segments.headline: A fireball

segments.text: And one spacecraft did. In nineteen ninety-five, NASA's Galileo mission dropped a small probe into Jupiter.
segments.headline: The Galileo probe

segments.text: It survived about fifty-eight minutes, sending data back as it fell, until the heat and pressure destroyed it.
Let's say you survive the entry. You're drifting down through the clouds, under a parachute.
segments.headline: The clouds

segments.text: The top clouds are made of frozen ammonia crystals, white and cold, around minus one hundred forty degrees Celsius.
segments.headline: Ammonia clouds

segments.text: Below are clouds of ammonia mixed with sulfur, and deeper still, water clouds, with lightning bolts more powerful than any on Earth.
segments.headline: Giant lightning

segments.text: Juno found that some lightning makes a strange kind of hail: slushy balls of water and ammonia that scientists nicknamed mushballs.
segments.headline: Mushballs

segments.text: And then there are the storms. The most famous is the Great Red Spot.
segments.headline: The Great Red Spot

segments.text: It's a storm wider than the whole Earth, with winds of more than four hundred kilometers an hour.

visual.label: winds in the Great Red Spot

segments.text: People have watched it for at least a hundred and fifty years, maybe more. But it's been shrinking. Nobody knows exactly how long it will last.

files: NASA's Hubble Shows Jupiter's Great Red Spot is Smaller than Ever (14005564929).jpg
visual.query: NASA's Hubble Shows Jupiter's Great Red Spot is Smaller than Ever (14005564929)

segments.headline: Shrinking

segments.text: Juno also flew over Jupiter's poles, where no spacecraft had looked closely before. It found giant cyclones, each wider than a continent, packed together in neat geometric patterns.
segments.headline: Cyclones at the poles

segments.text: And Jupiter's auroras, its northern and southern lights, are bigger than the whole Earth, and hundreds of times more powerful.

files: Jupiter and the Great Red Spot - Juno Perijove 7.png
visual.query: Jupiter and the Great Red Spot - Juno Perijove 7

segments.headline: Giant auroras

segments.text: Here's my first question. Did you know Jupiter has no surface, and you could fall forever? Tell us in the comments.

visual.q: Did you know Jupiter has no surface at all?

segments.text: As you sink deeper, the pressure grows and grows. The air gets thicker, then thicker still, until it's more like a hot ocean than air.
segments.headline: An ocean of gas

segments.text: Gravity here is about two and a half times Earth's. You'd feel crushed just standing still.
Thousands of kilometers down, the pressure turns hydrogen into a liquid. Deeper still, it becomes something strange: metallic hydrogen.

files: Hubble Takes Close-up Portrait of Jupiter.png
visual.query: Hubble Takes Close-up Portrait of Jupiter

segments.headline: Metallic hydrogen

segments.text: It flows like a liquid metal and carries electric currents. That's what makes Jupiter's huge magnetic field.

files: Jupiter and the Great Red Spot - Juno Perijove 7.png
visual.query: Jupiter and the Great Red Spot - Juno Perijove 7

segments.headline: Making a magnet

segments.text: Near the center, the temperature may reach about twenty thousand degrees Celsius. Hotter than the surface of the Sun.
And the core? Juno found it isn't a small solid ball, but a fuzzy, diluted core, mixed into the layers around it. Maybe from a giant collision long ago.
segments.headline: A fuzzy core

segments.text: Long before that, of course, you'd have been crushed, cooked, and dissolved into the planet. You'd become part of Jupiter.
segments.headline: Part of Jupiter

segments.text: Jupiter isn't alone. It has nearly a hundred known moons, a little solar system of its own.

files: Jupiter Family of Moons by Juno.png
visual.query: Jupiter Family of Moons by Juno

segments.headline: Nearly 100 moons

segments.text: Io is the most volcanic place we know, squeezed by Jupiter's gravity until its insides melt.
segments.headline: Io

segments.text: Ganymede is the biggest moon in the solar system, bigger than the planet Mercury.
segments.headline: Ganymede

segments.text: And Europa hides a salty ocean under its ice, with maybe twice as much water as all of Earth's oceans.

files: PIA19048 realistic color Europa mosaic edited.jpg
visual.query: PIA19048 realistic color Europa mosaic edited

segments.headline: Europa

segments.text: In October twenty twenty-four, NASA launched Europa Clipper to study it. It's due to arrive in twenty thirty, to find out if that ocean could support life.
segments.headline: Europa Clipper

segments.text: Here's my second question. Which of Jupiter's moons would you visit first: volcanic Io, giant Ganymede, or icy Europa?

visual.q: Which of Jupiter's moons would you visit first?

segments.text: So, would you ever want to fall into Jupiter? Radiation, fire, storms, crushing pressure. There's no part of the trip you'd survive.

files: Jupiter and the Great Red Spot - Juno Perijove 7.png
visual.query: Jupiter and the Great Red Spot - Juno Perijove 7

segments.headline: The verdict

segments.text: And Jupiter isn't only a danger. With its huge gravity, it has flung many comets and asteroids out of the inner solar system, though it has sent some toward us too. Scientists still debate whether, overall, it protects Earth.
segments.headline: Protector or troublemaker?

segments.text: Here's something lovely. Many of the colorful Juno images you've seen in this video were processed by volunteers, ordinary people around the world, from raw pictures NASA shared with everyone.

files: Jupiter and the Great Red Spot - Juno Perijove 7.png
visual.query: Jupiter and the Great Red Spot - Juno Perijove 7

segments.headline: Made by volunteers

segments.text: But from a distance, it's one of the most beautiful sights in the sky. On a clear night, it shines brighter than any star. Even with binoculars, you can see its four biggest moons.

files: A Dark Sky Full of Light (horalek-vst-milky-way).jpg
visual.query: A Dark Sky Full of Light (horalek-vst-milky-way)

segments.headline: Look up

segments.text: The best time is coming soon. On February tenth and eleventh, twenty twenty-seven, Jupiter reaches opposition, its closest and brightest for the year, up all night long.

files: Hubble Takes Close-up Portrait of Jupiter.png
visual.query: Hubble Takes Close-up Portrait of Jupiter

segments.headline: Jupiter's big night

segments.text: And next time you see it, remember: you're looking at a world with no ground, where it rains slush and the deep is made of metal.
Now my last question. What should we never get close to next? Tell us in the comments.
